name: Restaurant Papilio
review: This elegant restaurant done out all in white and with a beautiful high groin-vaulted ceiling is truly chic – you would never guess this space was once the château's stables. In the open kitchen, Jan Knedla and his team prepare a set menu comprising eight or ten courses. Inspired by the chef's childhood, the dishes lean towards regional ingredients and are presented in a modern and creative style. Seats at the Chef's Table promise interesting glimpses of the action. Service is friendly and professional; the chefs mostly serve the dishes themselves and explain the idea behind them. They offer a very well-stocked wine list and the wines are presented charmingly and with profound knowledge. Also recommendable: national or international wine by the glass or the tea experience as a non-alcoholic option. In summer there is a nice terrace.

name: Entrée
review: The Theatre Hotel not only wows overnight guests with its chic design, but it also offers an interesting dining experience based on an attractive modern concept. In the open kitchen, which can be seen from all over the restaurant, the team puts together modern dishes with light international accents. On the menu you can read for example "potato gnocchi, guanciale, whey" or "duck, chestnut, jerusalem artichoke, mandarin". There are three set menus, each building on the last with an increasing number of courses. The non-alcoholic beverage pairing is also recommended. In addition there is a good selection of cocktails.

name: La Villa Restaurant
review: A really lovely restaurant located slightly above the town… and it's not just the interior that is elegant and stylish – the food certainly holds its own. The classic/French-based dishes are subtly polished by the chef, as he brings in regional influences; this approach works particularly well with the saddle of fallow deer, for example. The best way to experience the handiwork of the kitchen is to opt for the set menu, "Le Pin". A vegetarian set menu is also available. At midday they only offer a simple lunch menu with two or three courses. Convenient: parking in front of the establishment.

name: LEVITATE
review: Featuring an interesting combination of Nordic techniques, predominantly Czech ingredients and Asian spices from the owner's homeland, the cuisine here is rather unique. The resulting dishes are full of finesse and pleasing contrasts - served in 12 or 18 courses. The location itself is something special: unassuming from the outside, it has a surprisingly chic interior. Upon arrival, diners are first led to the bar in the cellar for aperitifs and nibbles – a distinctive blend of exposed old brickwork and modern design makes for an atmospheric setting. Once in the tastefully furnished main room, you have the choice to be seated at the long "private table" or one of the smaller round tables. You can also pay a flying visit to the chef in the "Living Room" and indulge in a few small dishes. Excellent service – the exceedingly friendly team is always on hand - everything runs smoothly and efficiently. Tip: The famous historical city park Riegrovy Sady and the National Museum are within easy walking distance.

name: Štangl
review: A really interesting modern, open restaurant concept with a fully visible kitchen. They serve a three- or five-course menu based entirely on seasonal Czech produce. Without being fancy, the dishes are delicate and elegant, the flavours clear and well balanced. The atmosphere in the large, airy space on the first floor is pleasantly relaxed, and the charming staff are very professional and helpful. The responsible philosophy followed here is explained in detail – a film projected onto the wall introduces you to the producers. On Saturdays, a three-course breakfast using local and seasonal ingredients is also served. Tip: The Eska bakery located on the ground floor sells house-made bread, as well as preserved vegetables and much more!

name: Field
review: Two friends run this chic, minimalist restaurant in a stylishly understated way. Available in a longer or shorter form, their tasting menu comprises creative, well-balanced dishes with a strong focus on seasonal produce and Czech ingredients. Don't be surprised to see a sauce being flambéed tableside or smoke rising from a box! Worth mentioning are dishes such as ‘Crayfish, caviar, cream, Noilly Prat’ or ‘Veal, bone marrow, shiitake, Wagyu tallow’. The friendly and attentive front-of-house team, which includes a sommelier, will be happy to recommend and explain apt wine pairings. Two different versions of the shorter lunchtime set menu are served on weekdays and at the weekend, respectively. Notable details in the restaurant include the illuminated ceiling, various tools used for fieldwork, and the half-charred tables.

name: ESSENS
review: The Classical building of the Chateau de Frontiere, which cuts a fine, stately figure, is named after the erstwhile Austria-Morovia border. High vaulted ceilings supported by columns and sleek design create a picture of elegance, in keeping with the stylish location. Large arched windows afford a view onto the property's gardens. The set menu showcases precise modern creations made with regional and seasonal ingredients – they even grow their own vegetables. Good examples of dishes are ‘Cauliflower, ham, bay leaf’ and ‘Chicken, tarragon, Chinese artichoke’. To accompany the food, they have excellent wines to recommend, often from great local winemakers, especially from the Morovia region. In addition, there are also numerous internationally renowned names and a fine selection of champagne.

name: La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise
review: This iconic restaurant is housed in an attractive historical building in central Prague. From one side of the L-shaped room, there is a prime view of the chefs at work in the completely open kitchen. Seasonality and Czech ingredients are the order of the day and elegant, modern and well-balanced dishes are served in a set menu format. The sleek interior has chic features, including a vaulted ceiling, striking chandeliers and a glass wine cabinet. Cheerful and relaxed service and atmosphere. The distinctive shape of the tiles in the kitchen is reprised on both the restaurant floor and the menu.

name: Casa De Carli
review: Matteo De Carli and his wife Lenka Hermanová have been running their restaurant since 2012 after several stops around the world. The beautiful interior is straightforward and modern, with an open show kitchen and a walk-in wine fridge worth seeing as well as a wine fridge wall. Flavoursome cooking has a subtle North Italian bias, and the breads, pastas and ice creams are homemade. Make sure to consider the daily specials - the turbot in puff pastry crust, for exapmle, is a delight! Or let patron and chef Matteo surprise you with a 5-, 6- or 7-course tasting menu. In front of the house there are tables on the cobbled street. Tip: chef's table for max. 8 people in the basement - here the chef cooks right in front of you in a private setting.

name: Nebo
review: On the fifth floor of the Hilton Rijeka Costabella, as soon as you step out of the lift you are immediately captivated by a spectacular view: the Adriatic, the coastline and the wild island of Cres stand out unfiltered thanks to the long glass wall that encompasses the entire room, with its contemporary, minimalist design. Chef Gabriela Filca leads the kitchen brigade with confidence and talent, presenting a contemporary interpretation of Croatia's culinary heritage that draws equally from the country's coastal and inland traditions through a single tasting menu available in several lengths. Traditional ingredients such as lamb, catch of the day, or typical products such as trout, nettles and strawberries are reinterpreted with impeccable technique, seeking the ultimate balance between taste and aesthetic beauty. The service is professional and attentive, and a curated wine list, which also reaches out internationally, adds to the experience.

name: Cap Aureo
review: Chef Jeffrey Vella’s cuisine stands out for its strong personality, deep attention to the local area, and the use of carefully selected ingredients sourced from within a 50-kilometer radius. His cooking harmoniously unites the flavors of Croatia’s coast with the intense aromas of the hinterland. The menu, which the chef describes as a true journey, guides guests through seasonal delicacies with tasting courses of different lengths, offering the freedom to customize a bespoke gastronomic experience. Standout dishes include Adriatic lobster with charcoal-roasted cabbage and an intense, nuanced mushroom course. The wine list is curated and well-structured, with traditional, predominantly Croatian labels on the one hand and a vintage cellar with great international crus of excellent vintages on the other. Elegant yet informal service and splendid views of the old town complete a world-class gastronomic experience.

name: Alfred Keller
review: The town’s most luxurious hotel was designed in 1912 by Austrian architect Alfred Keller, whose name is today borne by the property’s gourmet restaurant. The terrace, overlooking the splendid bay of Čikat, provides the ideal frame for a refined gastronomic experience. In the kitchen, new Croatian chef Daniel Skokić continues along the path already laid, celebrating the finest local ingredients through modern and creative dishes of rich colour and nuance. The technical foundation is French, with international influences also present, in a proposal structured around an expansive tasting menu – adaptable across several formats – and a sound à la carte selection. Fish and seafood are the protagonists, though interesting meat alternatives are not neglected. An attentive and professional service and an excellent wine list, spanning local and international labels, complete the experience.

name: Agli Amici Rovinj
review: The restaurant enjoys a splendid seafront position along the elegant promenade of the modern Marina. A charming setting, enhanced by a spacious terrace – where dinner opens with refined finger food – and a breathtaking view over the blue sea dotted with lush green islets. As evening falls, the illuminated silhouette of the Church of St. Euphemia adds further charm to the atmosphere. The kitchen is helmed by Simone De Lucca, under the supervision of Emanuele Scarello, chef of the renowned two-Michelin-starred Agli Amici in Udine. The menu offers two tasting menus, Rovinj and Istria, dedicated respectively to the sea and the land, alongside an à la carte selection. In every proposal, great attention to the quality of the raw material and a precise, considered approach to its preparation are evident: few ingredients, each with a well-defined role, often celebrated in their entirety so as to ennoble even the less conventional parts. Among the most memorable dishes for our Inspector: the mussel and saffron risotto, rich in aromas, creaminess and fragrance, and the amberjack, courgette and saffron, played out through elegant contrasts of texture and flavour. For the wine pairing, it is well worth placing oneself in the hands of the knowledgeable sommelier, who can guide you through a selection of Croatian and international labels or suggest specially created original cocktail pairings.

name: Noel
review: Towards the end of 2025, chef Bruno Vokal, a key figure at Noel in the past, returned to the kitchen. His presence reaffirms the contemporary character of the restaurant, which offers a concise menu of creative dishes ranging across meat and seafood – both freshwater, such as the local trout that frequently appears on the menu, and from the sea – with occasional nods to national tradition, interpreted with sensitivity in the classic štrukli. The dining room remains true to its identity: modern, welcoming and enveloped in soft lighting, animated by a professional and well-coordinated service. The wine list is also of excellent standing, starting from Croatia and opening to international labels, with particular attention to France, presented with expertise by sommelier Kristijan Harjač.

name: Pelegrini
review: In the heart of the old town, the restaurant occupies Villa Pelegrini-Tambača, a Renaissance palazzo situated next to the Cathedral of St. James. Chef Rudolf Štefan, deeply knowledgeable about the region, distinguishes himself through constant pursuit of local products: he collaborates with top winemakers for exclusive wine production, makes his own olive oil, and prioritizes land and sea ingredients from Šibenik and its surroundings. Two tasting menus of four and six courses offer a modern reinterpretation of traditional Dalmatian cuisine with creative touches and refined presentations. Among the house signatures is lobster served on mushroom carpaccio with ricotta, sea grapes, and pickled cornichons: a surprising balance of sweetness and acidity. The wine list, with over 500 labels, is of considerable depth and breadth. In warmer months, dining is available along the external staircase with splendid views of the cathedral.

name: Boškinac
review: Surrounded by vines and olive trees, Boškinac is a refined country house with a boutique hotel, an oasis of peace in which to rediscover the unhurried rhythm of the island of Pag. The kitchen, which aims above all to celebrate the purity of its ingredients, interprets local tradition with creativity: Adriatic fish, lamb, wild herbs, vegetables and olive oil, partly cultivated or gathered nearby. Two tasting menus are offered, the Grande and Petite Experience, which tell the story of the local area with elegance and restraint. The cellar is equally central, being at the very heart of the family story: the Boškinac Winery, founded in 2000, draws deep roots from a centuries-old tradition. The wines, an expression of the rocky terroir of Pag, accompany the dishes with coherence, complemented by a carefully curated list of selected Croatian labels. In the warmer months, the terraces set among the greenery transform the restaurant into a romantic and evocative retreat.

name: Krug
review: An oasis of calm sophistication – with 12 seats on an L-shaped counter in front of the open kitchen – Krug is the creation of Chef-owner Karlo Kaleb. He and his kitchen are all from the local area and keen to celebrate its flavors and its produce. As they deliver each visually striking and creative dish to the diners, whether that’s the finger-snack of shrimp in homemade mascarpone topped with pickled kohlrabi or the ‘main course’ of delicious beef grilled over fire, they explain the full story behind it. Fish and meat are aged in the on-show cabinets, next to colorful jars of fermented and pickled produce. There are two evening sittings; the five-course menu is served earlier, while the full nine-course menu is reserved for those coming after 8.30pm.

name: Restaurant 360
review: In the heart of Dubrovnik's harbour, the slightly elevated restaurant affords splendid views of the sea and marina. The exclusive terrace, which stretches along the medieval walls and St. John's fortress, provides a lovely setting for a summer dinner. For a more romantic and intimate dining experience, choose one of the glass-fronted booths, known as “tents”, opposite the kitchen. Chef Marijo Curić, returning to his home town after significant experiences around Europe, holds true to expectations with technical and well-presented cuisine in which Mediterranean elements are enriched with Asian touches with a refined combination of French cooking techniques. Vacuum cooking, robata grilling, and well-mastered fermentations enrich each dish with a unique flavour. Two tasting menus are offered: one with the chef's iconic dishes and the other with the restaurant's classics. Try the snapper with beurre blanc, shellfish sauce and mussel and red shrimp cappuccino. The restaurant also boasts a superb wine cellar, with as many as 450 labels. The selection honours Croatia but is also open to the rest of the world, offering an excellent choice of international labels. The wine list is accompanied by customised wine pairings that may also include creative cocktails.

name: Monte
review: One ascends through the lanes and alleyways of the historic centre to reach the hidden stone courtyard of chef-patron Danijel Đekić’s birthplace, at the foot of the magnificent church of St Euphemia, the symbol of Rovinj. Monte is a place steeped in memory and identity: born in 1985 as a family tavern, it has evolved over time into one of Croatia’s most celebrated fine dining restaurants. The cuisine, innovative yet profoundly rooted in the territory, celebrates the finest regional ingredients with contemporary sensitivity and great attention to seasonality. Two tasting menus are offered: Flora, entirely plant-based, and Fauna, which encompasses Adriatic fish and selected meats. It is also possible to compose a shorter menu of three or four courses, choosing freely from the dishes of both principal journeys. The wine offering is also excellent, extending beyond Champagne to dedicate considerable attention to Croatian production. A final note of praise is due to the service: professional, warm and particularly attentive to the needs of each guest.

name: Dubravkin Put
review: Leave the bustle of the capital behind and take refuge in an oasis immersed in the greenery of Zagreb’s forest. At Dubravkin Put, a fresh and fragrant Mediterranean cuisine awaits, with particular attention given to raw fish. Among the offerings, all of great quality, the squid ink risotto with langoustine carpaccio stands out as a true delight. In the summertime, the pleasure is further amplified by the evocative outdoor area: a terrace immersed in green and surrounded by the lush vegetation of the park, where one may dine accompanied by birdsong. The cellar is also of excellent standing, with over 500 labels (part of the establishment is dedicated to an elegant wine shop). After the meal, a walk through the greenery is the ideal way to bring the experience to a close.

name: Harry’s Piccolo Poreč
review: Recently opened within a new five-star hotel, the restaurant follows the gastronomic guidelines of its two-starred sister establishment in Trieste, while the kitchen is entrusted to local chef Goran Hrastovčak, a man of considerable experience. The interiors are elegant and contemporary, and include a pleasant terrace ideal for cocktails and aperitifs, served with professionalism and enthusiasm by a young and particularly welcoming team. The gastronomic proposal is structured across two tasting menus and an à la carte selection, in a journey that weaves together sea and land, Italy and Istria, tradition and contemporary sensitivity. The dishes impress through colour, fragrance and harmony of flavour, as in the lobster with béarnaise sauce infused with kruškovac, black truffle and green pepper.

name: LD Restaurant
review: With the freshest catch, seasonal vegetables and local extra virgin olive oil, Marko Gajski builds a refined cuisine that cleverly combines Dalmatian ingredients, Eastern suggestions, French-style sauces and well-calibrated fermentations. The creative and flavourful dishes are the result of solid technique and recount a personal and consistent gastronomic journey. The service, which is always professional and attentive, takes place in the elegant contemporary room on the second floor, or – during the summer season – a few metres from the sea, with a romantic view of the water and surrounding islands. The restaurant's iconic dishes include shrimp gyoza with mousseline sauce and daikon – a refined and appealing dish that is always on the tasting menu. A vegetarian menu and a three-course formula are also available. The sommelier will guide you through excellent pairings, enhancing dishes with a selection of regional and international wines.

name: Korak
review: Surrounded by centuries-old linden trees and the rows of the family winery – which provide a backdrop for outdoor tables in fine weather – Bernard Korak has shaped a cuisine that is deeply tied to the land and seasonality. After important experiences alongside Three-MICHELIN-Star chefs such as Ana Roš and Massimo Bottura, the chef chose to enhance the traditions of the Plešivica region, where mountains blend with rolling hills covered with vineyards. His proposal consists of a single eight-course blind tasting menu, sometimes flanked by a shorter five-course version, to offer an intense and surprising dining experience. Creative recipes, but always focused on taste: a simple seasoned radicchio leaf becomes an explosion of flavours; the frog legs on spicy almond cream are delicious, as are the snails accompanied by bruscandoli and seasonal mushrooms. Rounding out the experience is impeccable service entrusted to Vera, the chef's sister, who is attentive and thoughtful in every detail.

name: Hiša Franko
review: Few kitchens reflect their chef’s personality as clearly as that of Chef Ana Roš. Her strong, determined character and infectious warmth find perfect expression in a single tasting menu where dishes possess bold, decisive flavors with no compromise. Each course is a discovery: local ingredients and Slovenian traditions converse with international influences, balanced through refinement, taste, and technical precision. The Orme menu traces this journey with distinctly characterized yet elegant dishes, animated by a note of vivacious and refined freshness. Dishes that captivate on sight through a meticulous, colorful presentation, while surprising at every bite. Among the most compelling offerings are the Cappelletti, “Saporito delle valli” with tonka and fig leaves: the creaminess of the sauce and balanced flavors create a singular experience. Among the house specialties, which are nearly always on the menu, don’t miss the corn beignet with fermented ricotta cheese and smoked trout roe, and the hay-baked potatoes with fenugreek and roasted yeast-infused sour cream – dishes that authentically express the chef’s identity. Completing the experience, the service is impeccable, orchestrated by a young, cohesive team who guide guests with professionalism, ease, and passion, eloquently describing dishes and suggesting targeted wine pairings. For overnight guests, breakfast is unmissable: generous, colorful, and meticulously composed.

name: Milka
review: Not far from the Austrian and Italian borders, overlooking a crystal-clear lake surrounded by mountains, Milka represents a magnificent gastronomic synthesis of the territory, interpreted with sensitivity and mastery by Chef David Žefran. His cuisine is built on local ingredients used in their entirety. The surprise menu unfolds naturally, marked by the rhythm of the seasons, while the kitchen brigade actively participates in service, presenting each course with detailed and passionate explanations. The culinary proposal is modern and creative yet doesn’t forgo intense and satisfying flavors, as in the spelt with Tolminc cheese cream, snails, and wild garlic, a dish that perfectly captures the bond between territory, technique, and taste. The desserts also merit special mention: they alternate delicate, fresh notes, such as Pearls of tomato water, basil, and sour milk, with more indulgent, enveloping creations, such as warm doughnuts with pork fat, hazelnuts, and apples. The wine list is a pleasure for enthusiasts: extensive and carefully curated, it reflects direct collaboration with numerous winemakers connected to the restaurant, eager to showcase their wines in a context of absolute prestige. For those wishing to extend the experience, refined hotel rooms are available.

name: Hiša Linhart
review: In one of the oldest buildings in the country, in the fully pedestrianised centre, chef Uroš Štefelin and his team welcome guests with genuine spontaneity. The gastronomic proposal is structured around three tasting menus – of five, seven, or nine courses – selectable at the time of booking. Regardless of the number of dishes, the journey celebrates the region's produce and recipes reinterpreted with contemporary sensitivity. Preparations such as krapci, ravioli filled with chestnuts and porcini, or sweetbreads, deftly served with finely cut vegetables, are but a few expressions of local tradition. In the surrounding area, it is well worth seeking out the typical porcelain in one of the small boutiques nearby, or the celebrated local chocolate, which also takes centre stage at an annual festival.

name: Dam
review: Located in Nova Gorica, slightly off the beaten track and a few kilometres from the centre, the restaurant welcomes guests into an urban-chic setting. You will be captivated by the relaxed atmosphere, pleasant music and a modern, reassuring culinary experience. No special effects here, just a balanced and sensitive indulgence for the palate. Among the dishes we sampled, the seafood rice with the fragrant aroma of oysters was undoubtedly our favourite: intense yet delicate, the smell alone evoked the sea breeze. Chef Uroš Fakuč is a constant presence in the dining room, personally overseeing the service and describing the dishes, ensuring that every guest enjoys a thoroughly satisfying experience.

name: Gostilna Pri Lojzetu
review: Situated on a small hill just outside Vipava, this elegant restaurant – in business for over fifty years – occupies a seventeenth-century residence that once belonged to a family of Venetian nobility. The interiors unfold across several rooms, each with its own distinct personality: particularly evocative are the stone spaces obtained from the original stables and kitchens of the historic residence. An enchanting dining room with a fireplace is the setting for a refined cuisine, where traditionally inspired dishes coexist with more creative and experimental proposals. Under the guidance of Tomaž Kavčič, among Slovenia’s most renowned chefs, the gastronomic proposal features a menu that showcases seasonal ingredients and products from the surrounding valley. The iconic and theatrical gin and tonic pudding remains an unforgettable experience, a symbol of the chef’s creativity and personality. A passionate sommelier guides guests through the extensive wine list, where Vipava Valley labels stand out: don’t miss the wines from Burja estate, among the zone’s most representative producers.

name: Grič
review: Luka Košir's restaurant and home can be reached by driving along hilly roads dotted with small villages and surrounded by lush green landscapes that offer a glimpse of Grič's rural character. The same beautiful view can be admired from the tables in the dining room-veranda, while culinary enthusiasts can sit at the table in front of the open kitchen to watch the team at work. The chef and owner interprets Slovenia in a creative key, offering two tasting menus – seven or eleven courses – to be chosen when booking online; once you arrive at the restaurant, you can then rely on his inspiration. The menu changes daily based on market availability, featuring fresh, high-quality ingredients: from vegetables grown in the restaurant's own gardens to eggs and meat (only in season) from the family's duck farm. The distinguishing feature of the cuisine is the use of dry ageing, applied to both meat and fish, which takes place in a dedicated space below the restaurant, along with fermentation and other processes. The result is a veritable compendium of culinary techniques, some of which are very creative and experimental. The selection of wines by the glass is conceived as an authentic pairing journey designed to enhance the dishes. There is also an original non-alcoholic pairing, based on tea, juices and artisanal preparations.

name: COB
review: COB stands for Cooking Outside the Box – a fitting description for the gastronomic philosophy driving this restaurant. Situated in the upper part of Portorož, it enjoys a magnificent view over the Bay of Piran, in a setting that unites modern, minimalist design with the warmth of a century-old wood-burning stove. At the helm of the kitchen is chef Filip Matjaž, supported by his brother Patrik, who coordinates a service that is both cordial and professional. The tasting menu conceived for 2026 takes Travel as its theme: the chef draws inspiration from countries across the world, reinterpreting their flavours and traditions through creative recipes crafted from excellent local ingredients. The experience is punctuated by stamps applied to a passport presented to each guest on arrival, in an original and engaging culinary narrative. Mexico, for example, is evoked by a taco filled with artichoke and crispy corn, whilst the guest personally assembles a tortilla stuffed with tuna tartare, sun-dried tomatoes, an onion crisp and a delicate spicy sauce. The result is a playful and surprising gastronomic journey, reflecting this young chef’s creative personality and imagination.

name: Pavus
review: The ascent to Grad Tabor castle in Laško, founded in the thirteenth century and, after centuries of history and varied use, transformed today into a gastronomic restaurant of romantic fascination, is well worth making. In this suggestive setting, self-taught chef Marko Pavčnik expresses a cuisine that is personal and unmistakable, little influenced by passing trends, and capable of celebrating the territory with creativity and contemporary sensitivity. Great attention is paid to quality: local ingredients, foraging, and whole-animal cookery. The dishes, with their clear and well-defined flavours, tell the story of Slovenia with elegance, as in the smoked trout with elderflower sauce. To appreciate the proposal fully, a tasting menu is recommended. The experience is completed by a rich wine list centred on Slovenian labels, among which the whites of Styria, a region renowned for wines of great character, stand out. In summer, the panoramic courtyard offers a truly singular atmosphere.

name: Galerija okusov
review: The setting of this excellent “Gallery of Flavours” is particularly striking: a park at whose centre stands an eighteenth-century Baroque manor, once the castle of Novo Celje. Decidedly more contemporary are the welcoming fine dining room and, above all, the gastronomic proposal, which takes local ingredients as its starting point and works them with technique and creativity. The choice extends between a concise à la carte menu and a tasting menu of seven courses, reducible to five. Among the most interesting dishes, the polenta with beef, a reinterpretation of a Slovenian classic, and the catfish mosaic with buckwheat, enriched by a beurre blanc sauce and leeks. With over 600 labels, the cellar is among the most remarkable in Slovenia.

name: Hiša Denk
review: Opened in 1972 and now run by the third generation of the family, the restaurant surprises guests with its modern, minimalist design and large glass walls that flood the rooms with natural light, from the moment they step inside. When booking, all you do is choose the length of the menu – three, five or seven courses for lunch, five or seven for dinner – while everything else is a surprise. In the kitchen, Gregor Vračko applies his deep knowledge of Styria, combined with remarkable creativity, offering a contemporary and unexpected interpretation of the region's outstanding produce.

name: Stand
review: A central glass-walled kitchen is the focal point of this eye-catching modern restaurant; a dining room sits either side, and there’s a chatty buzz to the room, which is helped along by the personable service team. The two experienced chef-owners are proud of their Hungarian roots and skilfully reinvent and modernise classic Hungarian dishes using a wide range of techniques. The wonderfully rich gulyás soup and the soft, flavoursome venison are hits, as is the ever-present somlói dessert. When it comes to wine, look to the Hungarian options – there are some great sweet Tokajis on the list.

name: Costes Restaurant
review: Elegance and sophistication lead the way at Costes, from the smart décor to the well-orchestrated service. Ask for a seat to the front of the main room for a feeling of space, then enjoy the eager anticipation as the sommelier presents an exceptional, mostly Hungarian wine selection. The modern 7 course tasting menu comprises memorable dishes which not only look stunning with their bright colours and artistic style, but are packed with vibrant, complementary flavours. Seasonality plays an important role here too, with the featured ingredients always informing you of what’s in season right now.

name: Babel
review: A city institution, Babel represents the perfect blend of tradition and modernity. Its walls still show marks from the 1838 Great Flood of Pest, yet it’s also a chic, stylish place thanks to passionate owner Hubert and interior designer Annamaria Dekany. The cooking follows in a similar vein, with the multi-course tasting menu comprising consummately seasoned, creative modern dishes which simultaneously exhibit references to their Hungarian heritage. Highlights include red shrimp with tomato and plankton, and guinea fowl with a steamed bun; be sure to go for the casino egg ‘add-on’ too.

name: Rumour by Rácz Jenő
review: After travelling the world, Chef Jenő returned home to open this unique restaurant. Located in the heart of the city, it comes with concrete walls hung with mirrors, and a 21-seater counter which wraps around the large open kitchen. Red leather stools and placemats provide colour, while a trendy soundtrack adds to the vibe. The set menu showcases elements from Jenő’s travels via a series of refined, creative, sometimes playful dishes that burst with flavour. These are matched by some serious wine pairings, with the Hungarian option offering some wonderfully unique, bespoke choices.

name: Salt
review: Within a boutique hotel sits this small, sophisticated restaurant, whose open kitchen forms an integral part of the stylishly lit room. Shelves are full of jars containing colourfully preserved foraged fruits, vegetables and herbs, and the butter, lardo and Mangalitsa ham are all produced in-house. The surprise set menu is made up of intricate, exquisitely constructed dishes – many of which are updated versions of classic Hungarian recipes – and tables all face the wood-clad ‘pass’, where the chefs assemble the dishes in front of your eyes with skill and dexterity.

name: Pajta
review: Pajta means ‘barn’, which is where it all began for Flóra and Ferenc – in the small barn beside this glass-fronted restaurant. The whole complex has a natural feel, from the beautiful meadow to the two-storey, nature-inspired forest lodges 1km down the road (they arrange transportation). Menus change with the seasons and perfectly reflect the area, championing produce from Őrség in historical Hungarian dishes. Fermenting and pickling are a feature, adding a welcome punch to the flavour-packed creations. Neighbouring Austria and Slovenia join Hungary for a tri-country wine pairing experience.

name: essência
review: Portuguese Chef-Owner Tiago and his Hungarian wife Éva have created a warmly run and deliciously different restaurant in the heart of the city. A bright front room with arched windows leads past the open kitchen to a more intimate room where patches of blue and white tiling hint at Tiago’s heritage. At dinner, pick from 5 or 7 courses – some have choices, allowing you to lead with either Portuguese or Hungarian influences, or to combine them for the best of both worlds. The interesting, flavour-packed dishes are poised and elegant, and Tiago has a deft touch when it comes to seasoning.

name: Borkonyha Winekitchen
review: While it would be easy to do, to pass by this unassuming-looking restaurant near the Basilica would be a mistake. The kitchen here sources top-class ingredients, treats them with the utmost respect and allows them to shine. Subtle Hungarian influences run throughout dishes which are well-conceived, skilfully executed and have a notable intensity of flavour. There is an à la carte, but go for the tasting menu for the best experience. Wines are key here too: they offer 100 labels, including some of Hungary’s top producers, with many available by the glass.

A pastel blue townhouse plays host to this series of intimate, elegant dining rooms, but many favour a spot in the striking glass-enclosed terrace overlooking the street. The multi-course menu opens with dishes inspired by the chef’s global travels, before moving on to offer refined versions of more local recipes. Beautifully presented, wonderfully flavoured Hungarian produce might include Danube salmon – accompanied by caviar, butter sauce and dill – or aged Mangalitsa ham with white asparagus, morels and chervil. Charming service and an impressive wine cellar add to the experience, as do the luxurious bedrooms.

name: Under Grain
review: Housed within the stylish Rosselli Hotel, on one of Valletta’s most elegant streets, Under Grain welcomes guests into a setting as sophisticated as its cuisine. The restaurant occupies the building’s historic lower level, where diners pass by the kitchen before entering a dining room crowned by a vaulted stone ceiling. Inspired by the tailor shops that once lined Merchant Street, the concept is woven throughout, from sewing-pattern menus to displays of garments, and even the pincushion used to present the bill. The offering is fully à la carte, with the option for guests to create their own tasting menu, reflecting the chef’s distinctly creative approach. At times, he ventures into bold, unexpected combinations – as in one of his signature dishes pairing mussels with sweet Gorgonzola and passion fruit – while at others he embraces more classic flavours. Even the bread course is memorable, evoking the chef’s childhood snacks. The wine list is thoughtfully curated and rich in gems from around the world, with a particular focus on Italy and France, alongside an excellent by-the-glass selection.

name: Rosamì
review: Overlooking Balluta Bay, Rosamì occupies a beautiful Maltese-style villa, whose first floor, pleasantly sheltered from the street below, houses a classic, stylish restaurant, with a distinctly romantic edge. The cuisine, now helmed by a youthful yet highly experienced Italian chef, showcases dishes with an international twang presented in two surprise tasting menus: one six course and the other eight, both flanked by a selection of appetisers and local cheeses from small producers - a delightful way to experience Malta’s artisanal excellence. The service is highly professional, courtesy of staff whose in-depth knowledge enables them to explain each dish with confidence. The wine list features vintages from around the world alongside local wines and an excellent selection available by the glass.

name: Fernandõ Gastrotheque
review: Temporary closed for relocation. Tucked away in one of Sliema’s quiet side streets, this small restaurant has become something of a beacon for fine dining in Malta. The cuisine is showcased through two tasting menus of five or seven courses, while the dishes evolve with the seasons. Our Inspector particularly enjoyed the house-made agnolotti filled with pecorino, served with Delica pumpkin, pine nuts and mostarda di Cremona, as well as the seabass escalope with leeks, preserved lemon, capers and kombu seaweed. Seamless, attentive service and an excellent wine list, featuring over 700 labels and numerous by-the-glass options, including premium vintages, provide the finishing touches to a refined dining experience.

name: Le GV
review: The lavish rooftop restaurant on the eleventh floor of the 1926 Le Soleil Hotel draws inspiration from the carriages of the Orient Express, creating an atmosphere that is both glamorous and steeped in history. In the warmer months, guests can also enjoy a panoramic terrace overlooking the city. In the open kitchen, chefs Andrew Borg and David Tanti craft a concise yet compelling selection of dishes, blending creativity with an international flair. While the menu may appear limited, the quality is anything but. Among the most popular dishes are the cured scallops with kombu, fennel and fresh yuzu, as well as the veal sweetbreads with beetroot, lobster XO and green pepper sauce. The dessert offering features just one option, but it unfolds into two or three indulgent, beautifully executed small portions – including a whisky zabaglione with butter-soaked brioche for dipping that is truly irresistible.

name: ION Harbour by Simon Rogan
review: Located on the seafront, on the fourth floor of the exclusive Iniala Harbour House, ION Harbour offers warm, precise service led by a youthful team, breathtaking views and truly exceptional cuisine. Chef Simon Rogan, holder of three Michelin stars at his Lake District restaurant L’Enclume in the UK, is behind the concept, while resident chef Christian Cali executes a complex and creative menu. The cuisine follows Rogan’s celebrated farm-to-table philosophy, using produce grown, reared or caught in the Maltese Islands whenever possible. The restaurant offers one tasting menu available at both lunch and dinner – alongside a shorter option at lunchtime – showcasing local ingredients and often highlighting individual producers. The impressive, 500-strong wine cellar is explored through curated tasting journeys, with an extensive selection also available by the glass. For the best experience, and to fully enjoy the spectacular views, request a table by the terrace windows, which are covered and heated in winter.

name: Noni
review: In 2017, chef Jonathan Brincat transformed a centuries-old house into a restaurant, naming it after his own nickname: Noni. A small staircase takes you down to the main dining room, set beneath a stone barrel-vaulted ceiling. Guests can choose between a full tasting menu or a shorter version. Either way, the experience offers a vivid, personal journey through the flavours of Malta: seasonal, mostly local ingredients, flanked by a menu map that pinpoints the locations of their suppliers, and traditional dishes reworked with a creative, contemporary slant. A standout example is their modern take on the classic Maltese fish soup, aljotta. The catch of the day is cooked separately, skin-on, then placed on a rich tomato and herb cream. At the table, the attentive staff pours the aromatic soup around the fish (generously seasoned with garlic, naturally), while a side bowl holds slightly spicy rice with pieces of puffed fish. Connoisseurs will appreciate the “Cellar” section, devoted to vintage whites and reds.

name: De Mondion
review: De Mondion delivers a stylish dining experience that fully matches the magnificent, fortified city of Mdina in which it is set. The gourmet restaurant occupies the top floor of the charming Xara Palace hotel, a 16C edifice. The indoor dining room is intimate and elegantly appointed, with lush carpets that lend it a soft, refined vibe, while the outdoor terrace commands a breathtaking view stretching over the island’s eastern side all the way to the coast. Chef Clint Grech and his team add a modern, light twist to Mediterranean fare, accented by a few French influences. An example: the tarte tropézienne paired with zabaglione at the end of the meal is particularly noteworthy. Technique is used thoughtfully, in a bid to achieve culinary harmony and balance. We particularly enjoyed the sea bass, with perfectly seared skin, flanked by pomelo, mushrooms, and an intense gutsy jus. In addition to swish, spot-on service, the restaurant is also proud of its savvily curated, well-stocked international wine cellar.

name: Nineteen18
review: It was all change in 2026 when Vita Bartininkaitė closed her Pas mus restaurant and returned to the kitchen here at Nineteen18, where she was joined by Justinas Misus. They may have all the latest techniques, but what makes the cooking so appealing is that it’s discernibly Lithuanian and makes great use of the country’s produce; even the herbs for the tea served at the end of the 10-course dinner come from Vita’s mother’s garden. Highlights include the succulent beef tartare with honeyed brioche, and refreshing sour cherry ‘snow’ served before dessert. Ask for the counter to get it on the action in the immaculate open kitchen.

name: Džiaugsmas
review: The discreet sign outside this period house adds to the intimate feel inside, while the dark, modern décor goes well with the easy-going atmosphere. There are two menus on offer but the best decision is to go for the tasting menu so you can try as many dishes as possible. The chef has a distinct style: his food comes with a certain creativity but flavours are always balanced, complementary and assured. Snacks like smoked eel beignet or cheese crisp with Baltic herring get your taste buds in the mood for heartier dishes like cod with fish broth sauce or beef tenderloin with shiitake mushrooms.

name: Red Brick
review: An hour out of Vilnius is The Farmers Circle, a wonderfully remote 1,730-acre working farm, and at its centre is this beautifully restored barn. Naturally, produce grown and reared on their farm features on the set menu. You start with beautifully rendered snacks, like beef tartare with egg yolk, followed by dishes that celebrate Lithuanian’s own culinary traditions, such as an updated version of balandeliai. The chef applies his own delicate touches but always with the purpose of highlighting the quality of the main ingredient. ‘Sleepy Horse’, the converted stable block, also houses 15 bedrooms.

name: Deep Roots
review: The roots of this heritage building sit back in the 17th century, but the moniker means much more than this, with the owners naming it to be: “About home, about connection, about roots. About where we come from and where we are going”. With this in mind, the experienced chef welcomes guests with a shot of Lithuanian moonshine and presents the multitude of dishes with lengthy explanations. Many ingredients come from their farm in Radiškis, and the nose-to-tail cooking is inspired by his childhood memories – in particular, his great-grandmother’s recipes. The highly original, boldly flavoured dishes surprise and delight in equal measure.

name: JOHN Chef's Hall
review: Situated within the A22 Hotel, this restaurant bears the name of John F. Kennedy, who stayed here back when he was 22. It’s an intimate spot, made all the more special by the addition of a striking red lounge where you both start and end your evening. The modern tasting menu reflects both the country and the seasons and is also playful in places, but never at the expense of flavour. The chefs present and explain the dishes themselves: maybe tomato with ricotta and redcurrants or potato dumpling with quail and gooseberry. Make the most of the bespoke wine pairings by booking a room for the night.

name: Max Cekot Kitchen
review: A red-brick former warehouse on the edge of the city plays host to this surprisingly sophisticated restaurant. You start downstairs with drinks and amuse bouches, before heading up the narrow spiral staircase for dinner, where Max has designed everything from scratch, from the furniture to the crockery. Numerous elements make up each of the original dishes on the surprise menu, with sweet, savoury and acidic flavours all balancing one another, and delicious sauces bringing each dish together perfectly. Home-grown ingredients, such as petunia, could accompany the likes of langoustine and pumpkin.

name: 180° by Matthias Diether
review: A modern harbour development just outside the city plays host to this stylish restaurant and its futuristic bar. The name refers to the 180° view from the U-shaped kitchen counter; sit here to watch the chefs in action or at a more intimate table looking out over the harbour. Ambitious, visually impressive dishes are the German chef’s hallmark and his detailed creations show a memorable array of flavour and texture contrasts. Choose between the tasting menu or an upgraded ‘Premium’ experience with caviar, truffle and cheeses. Warm, engaging service helps to create a relaxed experience.

name: NOA Chef’s Hall
review: Set within the same striking building as NOA is the stylish NOA Chef’s Hall, where you start your evening with an aperitif in the romantic lounge overlooking Tallinn Bay. The on-view kitchen is the heart of the restaurant – with the open fire used to great effect – and luxury ingredients are to the fore, be that Canadian lobster or preserved, locally foraged produce. The creative 7 course menu keeps you engaged from start to finish, with complex, highly original dishes packed full of complementary flavours and layers of texture. For one course you are invited up to the chef's counter.

name: Langouste
review: Located on the edge of the historic centre, this restaurant boasts expansive picture windows that frame stunning views of the Sava River and the city’s contemporary skyline. Talented and passionate, youthful Marko Derić, back in Belgrade after honing his craft in several European restaurants, is now at the head of a creative, razor-sharp kitchen team. Marko’s culinary approach is rooted in Serbian traditions and produce, to which he gives a modern twist, drawing inspiration from French and Italian cuisines. Diners can choose between a range of menus: a five-course fish menu, a five-course meat menu, a more elaborate eight-course menu that features fish and meat, a special lobster option and a concise à la carte lineup. In a unique touch, the chefs themselves present the dishes at the table, forging a direct bond between the kitchen and the diner. Every detail of a meal here reflects a deep respect for Serbia’s culinary heritage, thoughtfully and savvily reinterpreted through a contemporary lens.

name: Fleur de Sel
review: It is well worth driving the 60-odd kilometres from the centre of Belgrade to get to this fascinating property serving fine cuisine and excellent wines. The restaurant is situated within the Atelje Vina Šapat winery, amidst 12 hectares of vines. The dining room, decked in velvet upholstery and chandeliers, is elegant and classical with discreet modern touches, while its picture windows allow guests to enjoy sweeping views of the peaceful Danube, vineyards and surrounding lush green countryside. Talented chef Nikola Stojakovic brilliantly merges high-flying techniques he gleaned in some of France’s top restaurants with premium Serbian produce, including local meat and freshwater fish. His distinctive, creative approach involves presenting three successive versions of each savoury dish in a unique interpretation of the same main ingredient. For those willing to trade a view of the Danube for a front-row seat of the culinary action, a special table positioned directly in front of the kitchen provides a captivating and immersive experience. The wine cellar is a genuine Aladdin’s Cave, with over 500 labels ranging from the estate’s own production to outstanding vintages from across the globe. A fine dining experience in a class of its own!
